misconception_description: Student believes that variable names containing vowels can only store string values, while consonant-only names can store any type.

solutions.generated_code:
program JumlahMinMaks
kamus
  n, ndx, x, mn, mx : integer
algoritma
  input(n)
  for ndx <- 1 to n do
    input(x)
    if ndx == 1 then
      mn <- x
      mx <- x
    else
      if x < mn then
        mn <- x
      endif
      if x > mx then
        mx <- x
      endif
    endif
  endfor
  output(mn + mx)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student renamed variables to avoid vowels because they believe vowel-containing variable names can only store strings. Since the function works with numeric values (finding max/min and adding them), the student uses consonant-only names: 'nums' becomes 'nmbrs' (numbers without vowels), and 'sum' becomes 'rslt' (result without vowels). The student is confident this is the correct way to name variables for numeric operations. The code functions identically to the original - it's purely a naming convention based on the misconception, making it a benign stylistic difference rather than a logical error.
